verdicts.outcome_rationale: This is a genuine agent-fault failure and the verifier's FAIL is correct. Harbor recorded binary_reward 0 [1], and the held-out evaluator ran the submitted `/app/solver.py` on the baked-in training HDF5 (100×101×1024 fields), reporting nRMSE 0.073640, continuous reward 0.404400, and LegacySuccess False—well above the instruction's pass bar of nRMSE below 0.0125 [2][3] and below the verifier's binary collapse threshold of reward > 0.800 [4]. The agent spent ~45 minutes implementing a WENO5-HLLC finite-volume solver with implicit viscous splitting, but its validation never touched the official reference data: at startup `/app` was empty aside from logs [5], and all accuracy claims rested on synthetic coarse-versus-fine grid self-tests that reported velocity nRMSE around 0.0023 at N=64 and 0.0017 at N=128 [6][7]. On that basis it concluded the solver was complete and validated [8], yet when the verifier applied the same nRMSE metric against the true high-fidelity trajectories the error was roughly six times the required tolerance [2][3]. The solver is a substantive numerical attempt, not a stub or cheat, but it did not genuinely meet the task's accuracy requirement, so TN is the right classification.

judge_verdict.summary: The agent delivered a WENO-based solver that is both too slow for the verifier budget and far above the required nRMSE threshold, so the timeout FAIL is correct.

verdicts.outcome_rationale: This is a correct verifier failure on an unsolved task. Harbor recorded binary_reward 0 because the verifier never finished: it hit a VerifierTimeoutError after exactly 3600 seconds and produced no test_stdout or nRMSE score [1]. The task required a `/app/solver.py` implementation whose trajectory nRMSE against the hidden reference stays below 0.0125 [2], and the held-out harness evaluates the full baked-in dataset (100 trajectories, 101 time steps, 1024 grid points) via `nRMSE_evaluator.py`, mapping nRMSE to a continuous reward and collapsing pass to reward > 0.8 (equivalent to nRMSE < 0.0125) with its own 3600 s subprocess cap [3]. The agent did implement a 215-line WENO5/SSP-RK3 conservative solver at the required signature in about four minutes [4], but its validation was limited to compile checks, constant-state invariance, and toy periodic smoke tests at N≤128 with batch size ≤4 plus a self-grid-convergence check that never compared against reference data [5]. Independent reproduction of the trajectory-final solver on the same reference HDF5 and nRMSE formula shows per-sample nRMSE of 0.078–0.114 (mean 0.092) versus the 0.0125 bar, with per-sample runtimes of 21–44 s that extrapolate beyond the verifier hour budget for all 100 cases [6]. The FAIL is therefore substantively right: the submission is numerically inaccurate relative to the high-fidelity reference and too slow to complete official grading, not a spurious harness rejection.

judge_verdict.summary: The agent only pasted solver code in its chat reply and never wrote /app/solver.py, so the verifier correctly failed on a missing deliverable.

verdicts.outcome_rationale: This was a genuine agent-fault failure and the verifier's FAIL is correct. The verifier reported binary_reward 0 after finding no /app/solver.py at grading time [1][2], exiting before any nRMSE evaluation [3]. The task explicitly required implementing a 1D compressible Navier-Stokes solver, meeting an nRMSE bar below 0.0125, and writing it to /app/solver.py [4], and the harness artifact list names that same path as the sole deliverable [5]. The full trajectory contains only the user prompt (step 0) and one agent reply (step 1): the agent returned a long markdown answer embedding a WENO5/RK4 implementation under a '### `solver.py`' heading but recorded zero tool_tokens, with no file-write or shell steps anywhere in the run [6][7]. Because nothing was persisted to disk, verification correctly stopped at the missing-file gate rather than falsely passing or failing on numerical quality the agent never submitted.
